title: EVALUATION CARDS: An Interpretive Layer for AI Evaluation Reporting
claim: A multi-source reporting system is built as a staged pipeline that canonicalizes raw inputs into signals and reader-specific outputs.
layout: 4 source boxes feeding 4 grouped stage columns, left-to-right, color-coded stages
description: A flowchart with a row of four pale-blue source boxes across the top: EEE Datastore, AutoBenchmarkCards, Model Metadata and Entity Registry. A blue connector merges them and drops into the first stage. Below, four rounded stage groups run left to right: Ingest (violet, boxes A Load and B Explode), Standardize (violet, C Resolve and D Flatten), Compute signals (teal, E Per-row and F Group), and Output (orange, taller, G Dims, I Warehouse and J Views). Each box has a bold letter-and-verb title and a short description. Small arrows link boxes vertically within a group, and thick arrows link the groups horizontally. Color marks the stage type: violet for transformation, teal for signals and warehouse, orange for output. Group labels sit at the bottom of each panel.
caption: Backend canonicalization pipeline. Four sources feed four stage groups. Ingest (A–B): load and explode sources into one row per result. Standardize (C–D): resolve canonical identities and join benchmark metadata. Compute signals (E–F): per-result reproducibility and completeness flags (E); grouped provenance and comparability across sources (F). Output (G–J): materialize rollout hierarchy (G), emit warehouse parquets (I), render corpus, model, and benchmark views through Research and Policy reader modes (J). Colors: violet = transformation, teal = signals and warehouse, orange = output.
abstract: AI evaluation results are produced at scale but reported inconsistently across leaderboards, model cards, benchmark papers, and company blogs. The cost is interpretive: readers cannot reliably compare results across sources, identify what a report omits, or trace an aggregate claim to its underlying evidence. Recent efforts address isolated components but leave three gaps: they cover only narrow slices of the evaluation lifecycle and do not compose into a single interpretable record; they specify static representations that do not differentiate the questions different stakeholders bring to the same evidence; and they remain proposals on paper, lacking the extraction infrastructure required for adoption at scale. We present \EvalCards{}, an operational reporting layer that composes benchmark metadata, evaluation run data, and model metadata into a unified record. We (1) derive a reporting schema from a structured review of 52 papers and 10 stakeholder interviews, (2) implement four interpretive signals (reproducibility, documentation completeness, provenance and risk, and score comparability), rendered through reader modes calibrated to research and non-research audiences, and (3) deploy a monitoring tool that applies \EvalCards{} across 5,816 models, 635 benchmarks, and 101,843 results, surfacing systematic gaps in current reporting practice.
